content.title: About
content.content: Bread is a baked product made from dough of flour, water, yeast or sourdough starter, and salt. It can be homemade from a recipe or purchased at a bakery. There are many varieties: white, whole‑grain, rye, baguette, and more.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bread is one of the oldest foods, produced more than 14,000 years ago.
Over 200 different types of bread exist, differing in ingredients, leavening method, and shape.
In many cultures bread symbolizes hospitality and prosperity.
A traditional French baguette must meet strict dimensions: 55–65 cm long, 250–300 g weight.
Bread Day is celebrated on October 16th, honoring its role in nutrition.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Bread provides slowly digestible carbs that supply steady energy and help maintain blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in fiber (when whole‑grain)
items.content: Whole‑grain bread contains dietary fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B2, B3 and folate are involved in metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Bread provides iron, magnesium, phosphorus and zinc, important for blood formation and metabolic processes.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: Fiber and protein in whole‑grain bread help you feel full longer.

items.title: Gluten intolerance
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity may experience intestinal inflammation after eating bread.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White bread raises blood sugar quickly, which can be problematic for diabetics.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Some breads contain high amounts of salt, potentially contributing to elevated blood pressure.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Industrial bakery products may include flavor enhancers and preservatives that are not suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bread can be eaten plain, used for sandwiches, toasted, served with soups, turned into croutons, breadcrumbs, or used as a base for various dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bread in a cool, dry place in a paper bag or bread box. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag and thaw at room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with vegetables, no sauce is a dish made from cooked durum wheat pasta and fresh vegetables that are steamed or lightly sautéed without any sauces, dressings, or added oils. The vegetables retain most of their nutrients, while the pasta provides energy through complex carbohydrates.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is popular in low‑calorie diets because it contains no fatty sauces.
Vegetables such as broccoli, carrots, zucchini, and bell pepper are rich in vitamins A, C, and K.
Durum wheat pasta (semolina) has a lower glycemic index than regular white pasta.
In traditional Mediterranean cuisine the dish is often finished with a drizzle of olive oil, but the no‑sauce version highlights the pure flavors of the ingredients.
It can be easily adapted for vegan and gluten‑free diets by using gluten‑free or legume‑based pasta.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Pasta provides a steady release of energy, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and minerals
items.content: The vegetables supply vitamins A, C, K, as well as potassium, magnesium, and folate.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables and whole‑grain pasta promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Absence of sauce and oil makes the dish suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Phytonutrients in the vegetables (e.g., lutein, beta‑carotene) help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Wheat allergy or gluten intolerance
items.content: Durum wheat pasta can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Excess sodium from added salt
items.content: If the dish is seasoned with salt, monitor the amount to avoid high sodium intake.

items.title: Digestive discomfort from high fiber
items.content: Large portions of vegetables may cause gas or bloating in individuals with sensitive gastrointestinal tracts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta with vegetables hot or warm. Cut the vegetables into bite‑size pieces, steam or lightly sauté them in a dry pan, then toss with cooked pasta. Optionally garnish with fresh herbs (basil, parsley) or a splash of lemon juice for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared pasta with vegetables in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Pasta and vegetables can be stored separately: dry pasta in a cool, dry place; vegetables in the fridge in a vented bag with a small amount of moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: White beans (commonly cannellini or Great Northern beans) are legumes that are often canned in a reduced‑sodium brine. The beans have a creamy texture, a mild nutty flavor, and provide a good source of plant protein, fiber, and micronutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canning preserves most of the bean’s nutrients thanks to rapid heat processing.
Reduced‑sodium brine is usually achieved by replacing part of the salt with potassium salts or by using a milder solution.
White beans are a staple in Mediterranean dishes such as bean salads with tomatoes and olive oil.
Beans contain enzymes that may support gut health.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: A typical serving (about 130 g) provides roughly 7–9 g of protein, helping maintain muscle mass.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, aids blood‑sugar control, and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: White beans contain virtually no saturated fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Provides iron and magnesium
items.content: Iron supports hemoglobin formation, while magnesium is important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Reduced sodium content
items.content: Compared with regular canned beans, this product contains about 2–3 times less sodium, which is beneficial for blood‑pressure management.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive people; rinsing and cooking can help.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid may reduce mineral absorption; soaking and heat treatment lower its level.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add the beans to soups, salads, stews, pasta dishes, or use them as a filling for burritos and vegetarian patties. Before use, rinse the beans under running water to remove excess brine.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place. Once opened, transfer beans to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for up to 3–4 days.
